column2: Departure due largely to disagreements over the college's mission regarding the importance of art education, aggravated by financial difficulties.
Albers arrives at Black Mountain
The Bauhaus artist arrives at the end of November 1933; students and teachers expected a painting class, but Albers had never taught painting and had hardly ever worked on canvas.
The Alberses arrive in North Carolina
After the Bauhaus closes, Albers comes to North Carolina and stays seventeen years, shaping Black Mountain College's avant-garde art policy; Anni teaches weaving there.

The Asheville Citizen-Times headlines the arrival of “Professor” Josef and “Frau” Anni — a telling difference in titles. Anni, a recognized artist, is hired only as a tutor and serves as Josef's translator in the first months (she had had an English governess).
Black Mountain, North Carolina (grounds of a YMCA summer camp)

Two months after the opening, the Alberses arrive, recommended by Philip Johnson of MoMA to Rice and Dreier, who were looking for an art teacher. Albers had warned that he spoke no English; the college had warned that it could not guarantee it would exist more than a year. A founding event: they bring the spirit of the Bauhaus and of modernism.
The couple arrives two months after the college opens; a founding event that brings the spirit of modernism alongside the founders' progressive spirit.
The Bauhaus closes for good under Nazi pressure
The Nazis judge the Bauhaus too “un-German” in spirit and personnel; the Gestapo padlocks the doors of the school's last stronghold

After the Nazis come to power on January 30, 1933, and amid growing harassment, Mies van der Rohe announces to the students the closing of the Bauhaus, which had had to move to Berlin in 1932 after Dessau withdrew its funding.
The Berlin Bauhaus, moved there in 1932 in a desperate attempt to withstand National Socialist oppression, closes in July 1933
The attempt to oust Rice from Rollins College begins
Efforts to expel John Andrew Rice, an erudite classicist and an undisciplined teacher; the affair will culminate in the founding of Black Mountain College.
Rice is dismissed from Rollins College in March 1933, setting off the founding of Black Mountain.
Josiah Spurr's summer house, Alstead, New Hampshire

Joe Martin, a graduate of Haverford (1930) and Oxford (1932), with one term of doctoral work at Columbia, hears of the college through his sister Mitzi, a dissident Rollins student; disappointed with established teaching, he applies to teach English; after two interviews with Rice, he is hired.

“Mac” Forbes, a former Rollins colleague forced out a year before the crisis, invites Rice to his home. They talk for a long time without Rice mentioning money; toward the end, Forbes offers $5,000, and as Rice leaves, Mrs. Forbes adds another 5,000.
